chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Muawiya ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
The sacrificial camel is marked from the right side, and the man stands on its left side. Then he yokes it with an old slipper in which he has prayed.

key_terms.الْبُدْنُ: A specific type of sacrificial camel, typically one that is five years old
key_terms.تُشْعَرُ: To mark or brand by pulling out hair or making an incision
key_terms.قَدْ صَلَّى فِيهَا: In which he has performed prayer
key_terms.يُقَلِّدُهَا: He yokes or ties the neck-band (taqleed) to the animal

ai.seo_question: How should a sacrificial camel be marked and yoked according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi details the ritual preparation of a sacrificial camel, specifying that the animal is marked on its right side while the handler stands on the left, a practice reflecting the Shia emphasis on the auspiciousness of the right side in worship. The use of a slipper (na'l) that has been used for prayer to yoke the camel underscores the integration of daily devotional acts with major ritual obligations, linking physical purity to spiritual intent. This specific methodology highlights the scholarly tradition of deriving precise ritual etiquette from the Imams' practical demonstrations.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abu Umeyr, from Muawiya Bin Ammar, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:
‘The camel should be marked from the right side, and the man should be standing in the left side. Then he should yoke it with a slipper which he has Prayed in’.
en.sarwar: 6. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from ibn abu ‘Umayr from Mu‘awiyah ibn ‘Ammar who has said the following: “Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said,
‘Al-Bun is marked on its right side and the man stands on the left, then places something around its neck like an old shoe with which one has performed Salat (prayer).”’
